extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors studying classical Euclidean plane and solid geometry (advanced high-school or undergraduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: A sequence of classical Euclidean geometry problem statements, definitions, propositions (theorems) and exercises on circles, loci, coplanar lines, normals, parallelism, and solid (trihedral/tetrahedral) angles, together with demonstrations/solutions. Useful for practicing constructions and proofs in plane and solid geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems 26–125 (enumerated geometry problems and loci)
rubrics_metrics.description: A long enumeration of numbered problems (26 through 124 in this chunk) covering circle tangency, chords of contact, tangents, loci of points and lines under ratio constraints, properties of triangles and quadrilaterals, nine-point circles, Ptolemy's theorem converse, Pascal's theorem, construction problems (inscribing/describing circles and polygons), various proportionality and product relations among segments, locus problems, maxima/minima geometric problems, and many classical construction/proof exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each numbered item states a geometric proposition/problem often followed by a short hint, 'Dem.' (demonstration) or 'Sol.' when provided. Examples include: (27) chord of contact of a variable circle tangent to two fixed circles passes through a fixed point on the centre-connection line (proof sketch given); (31) nine-points circle touches inscribed and escribed circles of any triangle; (72) Pascal's Theorem with a demonstration; many locus and construction problems such as describing circles touching given circles or lines, constructing quadrilaterals with specified relations, etc. The problems serve as statements to be proved or constructions to be carried out; demonstrations or solution sketches appear intermittently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition i — Coplanar
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more lines are in one plane they are said to be coplanar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition ii — Dihedral angle
rubrics_metrics.description: The angle which one plane makes with another is called a dihedral angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition iii — Solid angle
rubrics_metrics.description: A solid angle is that which is made by more than two plane angles, in different planes, meeting in a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition iv — Vertex of a solid angle
rubrics_metrics.description: The point is called the vertex of the solid angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition v — Trihedral/tetrahedral/polyhedral angles
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid angle be composed of three plane angles it is called a trihedral angle; if of four, a tetrahedral angle; and if of more than four, a polyhedral angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition vi — Normal to a plane
rubrics_metrics.description: A line such as EF, which is perpendicular to a system of concurrent and coplanar lines, is said to be perpendicular to the plane of these lines, and is called a normal to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollaries: the normal is the least line from a point to a plane; lines making equal angles with a normal are equal; a perpendicular to each of two intersecting lines is normal to their plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition vii — Projection of a line on a plane
rubrics_metrics.description: If from every point in a given line normals be drawn to a given plane, the locus of their feet is called the projection of the given line on the plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition viii — Perpendicularity of planes (when meet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two planes which meet are perpendicular to each other, when the right lines drawn in one of them perpendicular to their common section are normals to the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition ix — Inclination of two non-perpendicular planes
rubrics_metrics.description: When two planes which meet are not perpendicular to each other, their inclination is the acute angle contained by two right lines drawn from any point of their common section at right angles to it—one in one plane, and the other in the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation notes why some definitions are placed later (depend on earlier propositions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop I — A segment of a right line cannot be partly in a plane and partly not
rubrics_metrics.description: One part (AB) of a right line cannot be in a plane (X), and another part (BC) not in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: produce AB in the plane and derive contradiction if BC not in it via plane rotation argument and axioms on coplanarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop II — Intersecting lines are coplanar
rubrics_metrics.description: Two right lines (AB, CD) which intersect in a point (E) are coplanar; likewise any three lines forming a triangle are coplanar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: rotate a plane through a common line until it passes through a third point and use basic definitions to show the lines lie in one plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop III — Intersection of two planes is a straight line
rubrics_metrics.description: If two planes (AB, BC) cut one another, their common section (BD) is a right line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: assume otherwise, construct lines in each plane and obtain contradiction via axiom forbidding enclosure of space by two straight lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop IV — Line perpendicular to two intersecting lines is perpendicular to their plane
rubrics_metrics.description: If a right line (EF) be perpendicular to each of two intersecting lines (AB, CD), it will be perpendicular to any line GH which is coplanar and concurrent with them. Thus EF is normal to their plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses squared-length relations and Pythagorean-style equalities; corollaries define 'normal' and properties (least distance, equal angle lines equal, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop V — Three concurrent lines with a common perpendicular are coplanar
rubrics_metrics.description: If three concurrent lines (BC, BD, BE) have a common perpendicular (AB), they are coplanar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: suppose one line not coplanar and derive impossibility using right-angle equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop VI — Two normals to same plane are parallel
rubrics_metrics.description: If two right lines (AB, CD) be normals to the same plane (X), they shall be parallel to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs auxiliary points and uses right-angle and distance equalities to deduce parallelism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop VII — Parallel lines and a transversal are coplanar
rubrics_metrics.description: Two parallel lines (AB, CD) and any line (EF) intersecting them are coplanar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: assume not and produce contradiction by enclosure of space by lines or by pointing out the line joining intersection points lies in plane of parallels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop VIII — If one of two parallel lines is normal to a plane, so is the other
rubrics_metrics.description: If one (AB) of two parallel right lines (AB, CD) be normal to a plane (X), the other line (CD) shall be normal to the same plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses coplanarity of lines, construction of right angles in plane and deduction of perpendicularity for the parallel line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop IX — Lines parallel to same third line are parallel to each other
rubrics_metrics.description: Two right lines (AB, CD) which are each parallel to a third line (EF) are parallel to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: consider coplanar vs non-coplanar cases; use construction of common perpendiculars and previous proposition on normals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop X — Equal angle between corresponding parallel line pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: If two intersecting right lines (AB, BC) be respectively parallel to two other intersecting right lines (DE, EF), the angle (ABC) equals angle (DEF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by constructing equal and parallel segments, showing corresponding triangles have three equal sides and therefore equal included angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XI — Constructing a normal from an external point to a plane
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: To draw a normal to a given plane (BH) from a given point (A) not in it. Solution: draw any line in the plane, drop perpendicular from A to that line, construct perpendicular in plane, then draw AF perpendicular to that to obtain the plane normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solution and demonstration given step-by-step with justification that AF is normal to the plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XII — Constructing a normal from a point in the plane
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: To draw a normal to a given plane from a given point (A) in the plane. Solution: draw any external point B and its normal BC to the plane; if BC passes through A done; otherwise draw AD parallel to BC through A to obtain the normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification: parallels to a normal are normals (use previous propositions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XIII — Uniqueness of the normal from a point to a plane
rubrics_metrics.description: From the same point (A) there can be but one normal drawn to a given plane (X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof splits cases: point in plane vs point above plane, and rules out two distinct normals by contradiction (equal right angles or parallel normals impossibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XIV — Planes with a common normal are parallel
rubrics_metrics.description: Planes (CD, EF) which have a common normal (AB) are parallel to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: suppose they meet, take a point on intersection, derive impossible triangle with two right angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XV — Parallel planes criterion via parallel lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Two planes (AC, DF) are parallel if two intersecting lines (AB, BC) on one are respectively parallel to two intersecting lines (DE, EF) on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs a normal to one plane and shows it is normal to the other, hence common normal implies parallel planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XVI — Sections of parallel planes by a third plane are parallel
rubrics_metrics.description: If two parallel planes (AB, CD) be cut by a third plane (EF, HG), their common sections (EF, GH) with it are parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: if sections met they'd produce an intersection point belonging to both parallel planes, contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XVII — Proportionality of segments cut by parallel planes
rubrics_metrics.description: If two parallel lines (AB, CD) be cut by three parallel planes (GH, KL, MN) producing triads of points (A,E,B; C,F,D), their corresponding segments between those points are proportional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses previous propositions about parallels and intersections; constructs planar sections and applies proportionality (reference to earlier books).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XVIII — Plane through a normal is perpendicular to the normal's plane
rubrics_metrics.description: If a right line (AB) be normal to a plane (CI), any plane (DE) passing through it shall be perpendicular to that plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: show every line in the plane DE drawn perpendicular to the common section is normal to CI, hence DE and CI are perpendicular planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XIX — Common section normal when two planes both perpendicular to a third
rubrics_metrics.description: If two intersecting planes (AB, BC) be each perpendicular to a third plane (ADC), their common section (BD) shall be normal to that plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not, constructing two distinct normals from the same point to ADC yields contradiction; hence BD must be normal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XX — Sum of two face angles of a trihedral angle exceeds the third
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of any two plane angles (BAD, DAC) of a trihedral angle (A) is greater than the third (BAC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses constructions in the plane and triangle inequalities, producing auxiliary equal-angle constructions and comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XXI — Sum of plane angles of a solid angle is less than four right angles
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of all the plane angles (BAC, CAD, etc.) forming any solid angle (A) is less than four right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by cutting the solid angle with a plane producing a polygon, adding inequalities of base angles of component triangles, and counting right angles; observation about re-entrant cases is given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises on Book XI — assorted propositions/constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of exercises applying and extending the propositions (draw planes parallel to a line, common perpendiculars as shortest distances, relations among face angles of trihedral angles, normals to planes from line intersections, constructing lines meeting two non-coplanar lines, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each exercise states a construction or theorem to be proved using the previously established propositions; these are posed without full solutions in the main text.
